Decision guide

Breast Enhancement Comparison: Intended Effect vs. Claims

This comparison helps distinguish a procedure’s intended effect from claims made in advertising. It does not suggest that a non-surgical procedure is automatically safer than surgery.

Home/Treatment comparison

At a glance

Intended effect, primary consideration and key limitation

Intended effect, primary consideration and key limitation
OptionPrimary considerationImportant limitation
Dermal fillersProduct-specific approved indicationsNot FDA-approved for breast enlargement
PRPEvidence for the particular intended useShould not be promoted as proven breast enlargement
Threads & mono threadsProduct-specific aesthetic indicationsNot established substitutes for breast augmentation
Sculptra / biostimulatorsProduct-specific authorised usesDo not assume suitability for breast-volume enhancement
Stem-cell approachesEvidence and regulatory status of the exact productMany marketed regenerative uses remain unapproved or investigational
Silicone breast implantsSurgical increase in breast volumeSurgery, implant-related risks and potential future procedures
Fat transferUses the patient’s own fat for augmentationVariable fat retention and a limited, individualised result

Choosing between options is not a matter of finding the “safest” label. It requires understanding your goals, your anatomy and health, the evidence for each intended effect, and the risks you are prepared to accept. A consultation with an appropriately qualified clinician is the appropriate way to reach an individualised view.
